intro: Rachmaninoff, who played his Prelude in C♯ minor, Op. 3 No. 2, in nearly every recital, recorded it for Edison in 1919. It begins with three low notes, A–G♯–C♯, and the soft opening chords return with enough notes to need four staves.

sections.label: A · Three low notes, pianissimo chords
sections.mNote: A–G♯–C♯ in octaves, followed by pianissimo chords

sections.label: B · Agitato in continuous triplets
sections.mNote: A descending melody inside continuous triplets

sections.label: A′ · Tempo primo, opening chords on four staves
sections.mNote: Tempo primo; both hands double the opening chords.

sections.label: Coda · Chords over a low C♯
sections.mNote: The bass holds C♯ while the upper chords change.

cues.title: Opening motto and ppp chords
cues.text: The motto A–G♯–C♯ is played in low octaves, ff. The chords that follow are marked ppp. The same three bass notes return beneath them and sound between the right-hand chords.
cues.evidence: Mutopia edition, after Bosworth and Universal Edition, opening through bar 3: octave motto and ppp answering chords. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/RachmaninoffS/O3/rach-prelude-op3-no2/rach-prelude-op3-no2-a4.pdf
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Sale to Gutheil, 1893
cues.text: In 1893 Gutheil paid the nineteen-year-old Rachmaninoff forty roubles for the Prelude, which he published that February. The piece travelled around the world. Years later, audiences still would not let Rachmaninoff leave the platform until he had played it as an encore.
cues.evidence: Robert Matthew-Walker’s notes for Hyperion CDA66081 give the fee, February 1893 publication and audiences’ demands for the Prelude as an encore. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6690_66081

cues.title: Agitato section, bars 14–16
cues.text: At the Agitato the right hand begins running triplets over a held low C♯. Within the triplets a melody descends by semitones, E–D♯–D♮–C♯.
cues.evidence: Mutopia edition, bars 14–16: Agitato, C♯ bass and descending chromatic melody within the triplets.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Siloti’s tour, 1898
cues.text: In the autumn of 1898 Rachmaninoff’s cousin Alexander Siloti took the Prelude on tour across Europe, England and America, where it became more popular than anything else he played. Rachmaninoff later teased his audiences in his deep voice, “Oh, must I?”, and came to call the piece “It”.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s BSO note on the Second Concerto gives Siloti’s autumn 1898 tour, the Prelude’s popularity and the composer’s name for it, “It”: https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6. Francis Crociata’s essay “The Composer” in the RCA/BMG booklet (1992), p. 24, gives the teasing “Oh, must I?”: https://archive.org/details/9-0023-sergei-rachmaninoff-complete-recordings-booklet-to-10-cd-set-rca-bmg-09026-61265-2-1992

cues.title: Return of the opening chords
cues.text: The opening chords return at Tempo primo, marked fff pesante, very loud and heavy. Rachmaninoff wrote them on four staves, two for each hand. The pianissimo reply to the chords now spans the width of the keyboard.
cues.evidence: Mutopia edition, bars 45–54: Tempo primo, fff pesante and four-stave piano notation.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: C♯ pedal and final chord
cues.text: The bass holds C♯. Above it the chords move by semitones, now separated by rests. The final C♯ minor chord is marked ppp, the same dynamic as the answer near the beginning.
cues.evidence: Mutopia edition, bars 55–61: C♯ pedal, changing upper harmonies and final ppp C♯ minor chord.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: Held bass under the Agitato triplets
transitions.from: A · Three low notes, pianissimo chords
transitions.how: The left hand repeats A–G♯, moves to C♯ and holds it. At bar 14, marked Agitato, the right hand plays triplets above this held bass, and the line E–D♯–D♮–C♯ descends through them. The long pauses between chords are gone, and the key remains C♯ minor.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia edition, bars 13–16; the established join corresponds to bar 14, marked Agitato.

transitions.title: Bass notes lead back to Tempo primo
transitions.to: A′ · Tempo primo, opening chords on four staves
transitions.how: The running chords stop on two enormous bass notes, A and G♯. F♯ minor over A moves to a G♯ dominant seventh, then resolves into C♯ minor at Tempo primo. The bass plays the opening signal again, and both hands follow with doubled chords, marked fff pesante.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia edition, bars 44–46; the established join corresponds to bar 45, Tempo primo.

transitions.title: Into the coda over low C♯
transitions.from: A′ · Tempo primo, opening chords on four staves
transitions.to: Coda · Chords over a low C♯
transitions.how: A diminuendo brings the doubled chords down to mf. The bass reaches C♯ and repeats it while the hands play shorter, separated chords above. The chromatic notes in these chords drop out one by one, and the passage ends on a plain C♯ minor chord at ppp.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia edition, bars 53–61; the established coda join corresponds to bar 55.

composer.epithet: Russian composer and pianist who earned his living at the piano in exile and whose music uses the sound of the bells of his childhood.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen and had recently graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 he sat in the audience and applauded.

His childhood had been less settled. He was born into a landowning family and grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated, his sister Sofia died of diphtheria, and his schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the choirs and bells he remembered all his life. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended that he move to Moscow to study with the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev, who was known for his strictness.
